..
As of 305 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain chances increase tonight into Sunday as the 
remnants of Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias move farther inland. There 
is a Slight Risk for severe weather Sunday.

Isaias is now a post-tropical cyclone centered over central AL. 
Meanwhile, a strong area of high pressure (~1035 mb) was located 
over interior portions of New England. This has resulted in CAD 
across the Mid Atlantic with the associated warm front across the 
Deep South and widespread cloud cover across the region. The 
remnants of Isaias will continue to track NE into Sun. As this 
occurs, the system will occlude and form a secondary surface low 
across the western Carolinas early Sun that will track NE across the 
local area late Sun afternoon into Sun evening. As this secondary 
surface low lifts NE, it will help lift a warm front north through 
the day.

Isentropic ascent has allowed for light showers aloft to continue to 
overspread the local area this afternoon. However, RH values were 
low with 50-60% RH common given temps in the low-mid 70s and dew 
points in the 50s for most (60s across far SE VA/NE NC). As such, 
most of these showers have been virga with only occasional, brief 
light sprinkles reaching the surface. However, as the low-levels 
saturate later this afternoon into tonight, RH will increase and 
rain will become more widespread from south to north. A
widespread, wetting rain is still expected tonight into early 
Sun. Rain could be heavy at times. However, models continue to 
show a lull in the precip from late Sun morning into early Sun 
afternoon. This lull should allow for destabilization to occur, 
especially if some cloud breaks become present. However, the 
degree of destabilization remains in question with the HRRR 
showing more widespread convection (and therefore lower 
instability) whereas the NAM, RRFS, and several of the WRFs show
lower coverage of showers and storms in the afternoon. Given 
the general model consensus for a lull in the precip, the HREF 
shows mean CAPE of above 1000 J/kg. The REFS is slightly low 
(700-1000 J/kg). In either case, this is plenty of instability 
(if realized) for October to cause severe weather.

CAMs continue to show either a line or broken line of supercells 
developing across west-central NC early Sun afternoon, moving NE 
with time into the local area by late Sun afternoon into Sun 
evening. This convection forms behind a mid-level dry slot which 
should aid in updraft growth and maintenance. Additionally, 
since this convection forms along a theta-e boundary on the SE 
side of a surface low, rich moisture will likely be in place 
ahead of the convection along with backed (SE) surface winds. 
This is also colocated with a strengthening LLJ which will add 
ample shear and helicity for rotating updrafts. As such, the 
threat for severe weather continues to increase with the main 
threat being a few tornadoes and/or damaging winds. SPC has a 
slight (level 2/5) risk for severe storms across the western 
two-thirds of the FA with a marginal risk along the coast. Given
the track of the surface low and more favorable timing, the 
greatest threat for tornadoes is across portions of south-
central VA late Sun afternoon into Sun evening. Storms should 
gradually weaken east of I-95 given the loss of diurnal 
instability. However, isolated severe weather could persist to 
the coast Sun night. The most likely timing for severe weather 
is from 2-10 PM. Will note that exact timing could change 
depending on the speed of the system as whole. 

This line marks the end of the severe threat. However, another round 
of showers appears increasingly likely on the backside of the low 
Sun night into early Mon morning. Rain could be locally heavy even 
with this round. Given the multiple rounds of convection, confidence 
in exact rainfall totals has decreased. The current forecast 
shows 0.5-1" of rain for central VA and interior NE NC with 1-2"
along the coast and across the western Piedmont. That being 
said, locally higher totals of 2-3"+ remain possible. WPC has 
maintained a marginal risk for excessive rainfall (ERO) tonight 
along the Albemarle Sound and Sun across far eastern portions of
the FA.

Otherwise, E/ENE winds of 5-10 mph inland and 10-15 mph with gusts 
up to 20-25 mph along the coast this afternoon increase to 10-15 mph 
with gusts up to 20-25 mph inland and 15-20 mph with gusts up to 30-
35 mph along the coast late tonight into early Sun. The strongest 
winds look to be along and just north of the warm front as it lifts 
north across the area. Winds become SSE/SE and remain breezy 
(especially along the coast) Sun afternoon. Given the retreating CAD 
Sun, highs may struggle to warm above 70F across the far NW Piedmont 
but should be able to warm into the upper 70s across south-central 
and SE VA as well as NE NC. A few locations may even reach 80F.
